findings.title: Options object implicitly enables rejectOnClear despite documented default false
findings.cause: When the first argument is an options object, destructuring defaults rejectOnClear to true at index.js:7. The README and type declarations both document rejectOnClear as optional with Default: false.
findings.impact: Users calling pLimit({concurrency: 1}) get different clearQueue() behavior than pLimit(1): queued promises are rejected with AbortError by default. Existing Promise.all workflows that only intended to discard pending tasks can now fail unexpectedly.
findings.evidence: index.js:6-8 sets ({concurrency, rejectOnClear = true}); readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 state Type: boolean / Default: false. Runtime probe output for pLimit({concurrency: 1}) + clearQueue(): "pending rejected AbortError".
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); limit(() => new Promise(() => {})); const pending = limit(() => 'ran'); await Promise.resolve(); pending.then(v => console.log('pending fulfilled', v), e => console.log('pending rejected', e.name)); limit.clearQueue(); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));"

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation condition at index.js:12 only checks the type when rejectOnClear is truthy: if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'). Falsy invalid values such as 0, empty string, or null skip the TypeError path.
findings.impact: Invalid options are silently accepted even though rejectOnClear is documented and typed as boolean. This can hide configuration bugs and make clearQueue() semantics depend on accidental falsy coercion.
findings.evidence: readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 require a boolean option. Runtime probe output: "0 accepted", " accepted", "null accepted" for pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}). index.test-d.ts:29 also expects non-boolean rejectOnClear to be rejected at type level.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, '', null]) { try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}); console.log(String(value), 'accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(String(value), 'threw', error.message); } }"

findings.title: limit.map omits the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper wrapper at index.js:108-112 passes the Array.from index only when Array.isArray(iterable) is true, and passes undefined for Sets, array iterators, generators, and other iterables.
findings.impact: The public API promises that mapperFunction receives the item value and its index for an iterable. Consumers using Set, generator, or iterator inputs get undefined instead, breaking offset-aware mapping and producing incorrect results.
findings.evidence: readme.md:78-85 and index.d.ts:29-43 say the mapper receives the item value and its index and is equivalent to Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)). Runtime probe with Set and array iterator produced [["a",null],["b",null],["c",null]] after JSON stringification, showing the index argument was undefined.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(2); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(new Set(['a','b','c']), (value, index) => [value, index]))); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(['a','b','c'].values(), (value, index) => [value, index])));"

findings.title: limitFunction drops all arguments passed to the returned function
findings.cause: limitFunction returns a zero-argument wrapper at index.js:124: return () => limit(() => function_()); The returned function never captures or forwards its call arguments.
findings.impact: Any limited function that depends on parameters receives undefined values. The documented reusable-fetch pattern and the TypeScript signature for (...arguments_) => Promise<ReturnType> are broken at runtime.
findings.evidence: index.d.ts:133-136 declares limitFunction as returning (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>. recipes.md:161-163 calls limitedFetchUrl(url). Runtime probe with limitFunction(async value => value) returned undefined for limited('input').
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async value => value, {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited('input'));"

findings.title: Infinity concurrency support regressed for constructor and setter
findings.cause: validateConcurrency now only accepts positive integers at index.js:128. The repository baseline implementation accepted Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY as a valid positive concurrency value.
findings.impact: Users can no longer choose an unlimited/no-throttle mode with pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY), nor can they raise an existing limiter to Infinity through limit.concurrency. Both calls throw TypeError before any work can be queued.
findings.evidence: git show HEAD:index.js shows validateConcurrency previously allowed (Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0. Current index.js:127-130 removes the Infinity allowance. Runtime probes output "threw Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up" for pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) and "setter threw Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up" for limit.concurrency = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { console.log(pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY).concurrency); } catch (error) { console.log('threw', error.message); } const limit = pLimit(1); try { limit.concurrency = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY; console.log('setter accepted', limit.concurrency); } catch (error) { console.log('setter threw', error.message); }"
